Beliefs within networks

Local evidence, persistent factions and the limits of Bayesian trust.

A small, reproducible study of agents with internal Bayesian networks. The main experiments share fresh observations with social neighbours. Common-evidence experiments are retained as separate mathematical cross-checks.

Local evidence creates a transient disagreement peak

In the five-node networked model, each active agent conducts 10 Bernoulli trials, then shares the complete fresh counts with its neighbours. The cycle gives each agent two neighbours; the complete graph gives it 59. Both start with the same 60-agent Halton population used in the shared-evidence control.

On the cycle, mean joint JS rises from 0.252992 to 0.323707 in one round, then falls towards 0.253919. Complete-network agents receive the same large batch and approach the endpoint in one round. The comparison therefore includes a large difference in evidence volume, shown explicitly below.

Agreeing about H2 is not agreeing about everything. All eight runs settle H2, but differences about the upstream hypotheses remain. The eventual whole-network divergence is close to the shared-evidence conditioning limit, not zero. These are finite-horizon observations, not a proof that any general social-network model must converge.

The slight increase is real—and interpretable

The original shared-evidence five-node instance has joint JS 0.252992 → 0.253919, a 0.366% increase. Its ordered-pair mean joint KL also increases: 1.396911 → 1.402020. This is not an artefact of using JS, rounding error or different observations reaching different agents: every agent in this control receives the same evidence.

The prescribed all-positive sequence approaches conditioning on H2 = true. For these priors, that outcome raises joint JS slightly; H2 = false instead lowers it to 0.245135. The original control contains no random data draw. Its increase is a property of the selected population and selected evidence outcome.

Across 100 independently sampled uniform-prior populations, 22 increased; across 100 scrambled-Halton populations, 3 increased. Both sets had a negative average change. Changing the unscrambled Halton population size also changes the sign: 15 and 120 agents decrease, while 30 and 60 increase. These counts describe this sensitivity check, not a universal probability of divergence.

The posterior was checked against R bnlearn/gRain, against a direct normalized likelihood calculation, and the JS calculation against SciPy. Both sides of the exact KL and weighted-JS chain identities agree to below 6 × 10⁻¹⁵. Shared downstream CPTs also make the full-joint JS equal to the JS of the root distributions here; deleting an irrelevant array axis is not the explanation.

What the expectation result actually guarantees

Directed KL obeys the chain-rule identity below. The expectation uses the first agent’s predictions for D. A realised observation can increase divergence; the expectation cannot. The inequality is strict only if the two predictive distributions of D differ.

ED ∼ P[ KL(P(X | D) || Q(X | D)) ]
= KL(P(X,D) || Q(X,D)) − KL(P(D) || Q(D)).

For fresh data generated by a common likelihood, the initial joint KL over (X,D) equals the initial KL over X. For an existing observed node, X denotes the remaining variables. Neither statement assumes that the realised posterior divergence must fall.

JS has a related identity, but its mixture weights update. Let m(d) = [p(d)+q(d)]/2 and w(d) = p(d)/[p(d)+q(d)]. Then:

JS½(P(X,D), Q(X,D))
= JS½(P(D), Q(D)) + Σd m(d) JSw(d)(P(X | d), Q(X | d)).

Ordinary JS sets both weights back to ½ after every observation. That is a different quantity. Consequently, the KL expectation result does not immediately establish contraction of equal-weight posterior JS under the shared-CPT model.

A concrete equal-weight JS counterexample inside the five-node population

Agents 34 and 47 (zero-based) have root priors (H1,H4,H5) = (0.765625, 0.901235, 0.088) and (0.046875, 0.197531, 0.768), with the same downstream CPTs. They assign H2 = true probabilities 0.387590 and 0.594032.

Both agents expect an increase in ordinary JS. The directed-KL and properly weighted-JS identities still hold. Across this population, 383 of 1,770 pairs have an increased expected equal-weight JS under their pair-mixture predictive distribution, although the population average decreases.

The same pair obeys the directed-KL theorem

The directions use different predictive measures. A population’s symmetrized KL summary should not silently be substituted into an identity for a single directed KL under its first agent’s predictions.

Implication for the paper: retain the distinction between realised outcomes and expectations; state the directed-KL expectation theorem precisely; and replace the immediate extension to ordinary JS with the weighted identity or a suitably restricted claim. This affects the information-theoretic guarantee. It does not remove the demonstrated possibility of Bayesian faction formation.

Here “shared conditional relationships” means shared parent-to-child CPTs, as in the implemented examples. It does not mean agreement on every reverse conditional probability: those generally differ when priors differ. A revised theorem should make this distinction explicit.

The social-network intuition is visible in the data

For the one-belief cycle, mean JS about H rises from 0.0945 to 0.1512 at round 9 before falling nearly to zero. The H + S cycle peaks at 0.1412 at round 8. In each cycle condition, 11 of 12 runs rise above their initial disagreement within the first ten rounds. The complete-network averages instead peak at the start, although some individual runs still increase.

Signals against S lowered final mean belief in high-quality evidence to 0.265, while final mean H remained 0.999. Signals against H left mean H at 0.726, with substantial within-run dispersion. These contrasts are illustrative; 12 runs with adaptive experimentation do not establish a universal effect of either propaganda mechanism.

A Bayesian model can be honest about what it cannot identify

With uninformative reporting as the alternative, final average trust was 0.839 for actually reliable sources and 0.175 for uninformative sources. Eleven of twelve mixed-source runs ended with every agent above H = 0.95; one run stopped experimenting. Learning trust was useful, but it did not guarantee success.

The opposite-reporting case has an exact symmetry. With prior P(R = reliable) = ½, conditional on the reported trial counts, every source’s entire report history has the same marginal likelihood under H and not-H: flipping H and R together preserves the report likelihood. Marginalizing R therefore gives Bayes factor 1 for H. More testimony alone cannot break that symmetry.

½ L(reports | H, reliable) + ½ L(reports | H, opposite)
= ½ L(reports | not-H, reliable) + ½ L(reports | not-H, opposite).

Private evidence can change H, and beliefs about H can change trust. But testimony does not add information about H in this exact symmetric setup. All 77 agents initially at H ≤ 0.5 across the twelve runs never experiment and retain their initial H belief. For the 108 actually reliable agents, the saved report counts also give their private counts: a direct private-only posterior matches every saved H trajectory within 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁵.

A non-symmetric reliability prior, independently calibrated source, or forced exploratory trials could break aspects of this trap. Those interventions were not simulated in this approved batch.

Methods, scope and reproducibility

The initial batch contained ten scenarios × twelve seeds (1729–1740) × twelve agents × eighty rounds, with ten trials per active agent and ε = 0.05. All used fixed horizons. The additional five-node comparison used sixty agents, two topologies, four seeds and forty rounds, with observation probabilities 0.35/0.65. Both batches used exact Python inference; the shared-evidence posterior audit additionally used R bnlearn 5.2.1 and gRain 1.4.6.

Simulations use the actual PolyGraphs operations on DGL graphs. Every active source generates fresh counts once, sends them unchanged to its outgoing neighbours, and uses its own data once. Received reports are not re-forwarded. Communication is local, not filtered by agreement or report content. All agents decide from pre-round beliefs and update after the round’s evidence is generated.

KL summaries average directed KL over all ordered distinct agent pairs, equivalently half the Jeffreys divergence averaged over unordered pairs. Full log posteriors were retained in the networked five-node runs, so underflow of tiny probabilities does not create spurious infinite KL. For JS about H in the initial batch, probability roundoff of at most 7.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ was clipped to [0,1]; no substantive probability mass was smoothed. The raw saved arrays remain available.

The model-selection and population comparisons are exploratory and small. There are no significance claims, no parameter search for attractive outcomes and no hidden discarded seeds. Different network degrees change the amount of evidence received, so topology and evidence volume are not isolated. Stable polarization, calibration and long-run convergence would require additional designs.
